'''Vivienne Lucille Malone-Mayes''' ({{nee}} Malone; February 10, 1932 – June 9, 1995) was an American [[mathematician]] and [[professor]]. Malone-Mayes studied properties of functions, as well as methods of teaching mathematics.<ref name=Vivienne>[https://baylorarchives.cuadra.com/cgi-bin/starfetch.exe?PIpsiDv9o8MzDKp2AZdNCsP7qUJk2LL6JHEA1IyRBQLD2CJaBCTla6nH8ySYwGEvqPBKGb.Y5jKMdmg1xFaB.sY8jKv1k84kaFhY5SBKdm0/0000nz.xml Vivienne Malone-Mayes Papers] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181028042831/https://baylorarchives.cuadra.com/cgi-bin/starfetch.exe?PIpsiDv9o8MzDKp2AZdNCsP7qUJk2LL6JHEA1IyRBQLD2CJaBCTla6nH8ySYwGEvqPBKGb.Y5jKMdmg1xFaB.sY8jKv1k84kaFhY5SBKdm0/0000nz.xml |date=2018-10-28 }} #2072, [[The Texas Collection]].</ref> She was the fifth African-American woman to gain a PhD in mathematics in the United States, and the first African-American member of the faculty of [[Baylor University]].
{{Portal|United States}}

==Early life and education==
Vivienne Lucille Malone was born on February 10, 1932, in [[Waco, Texas]], to Pizarro and Vera Estelle Allen Malone.<ref name="Vivienne" /> She encountered educational challenges associated with growing up in an African-American community in the South, including racially [[School segregation in the United States|segregated schools]],<ref name="Warren 1999">{{cite book|last1=Warren|first1=Wini|title=Black women scientists in the United States|date=1999|publisher=Indiana University Press|location=Bloomington, Ind. [u.a.]|isbn=0253336031|pages=[https://archive.org/details/blackwomenscient00warr/page/193 193]–195|url=https://archive.org/details/blackwomenscient00warr|url-access=registration|quote=wini warren black women scientists.}}</ref> but the encouragement of her parents, both educators, led her to avidly pursue her own education.

She graduated from A. J. Moore High School in 1948. She entered [[Fisk University]] at the age of 16 where she earned a bachelor's degree (1952) and a master's degree (1954). Vivienne switched from medicine to mathematics after she began studying under [[Evelyn Boyd Granville]] and [[Lee Lorch]]. Granville was one of the first of five African-American women to earn her Ph.D. in mathematics.<ref name=Vivienne/>

==Career==
After earning her master's, she chaired the Mathematics department at [[Paul Quinn College]] for seven years and then at [[Bishop College]] for one year before deciding to take further graduate mathematics course.<ref name=BU>[https://www.math.buffalo.edu/mad/PEEPS/mayes_vivienne_malone.html    State University of New York at Buffalo website, ''Black Women in Mathematics: Vivienne Malone Mayes'', article by Scott W. Williams, 2008]</ref> She was refused admission at [[Baylor University]] due to segregation and instead attend summer courses at the [[University of Texas]]. After another year of teaching she decided to attend the University of Texas full-time as a graduate student. She was the only African American and only woman in the class, and at first her classmates ignored her. She was not allowed to teach, was unable to attend professor [[Robert Lee Moore]]'s lectures, and could not join off-campus meetings because they were held in a coffee shop which could not, under Texas law, serve African Americans. She wrote, "My mathematical isolation was complete", and that "it took a faith in scholarship almost beyond measure to endure the stress of earning a Ph.D. degree as a Black, female graduate student".<ref name="Malone-Mayes">{{cite book|last1=Case|first1=Bettye Anne|author1-link=Bettye Anne Case|last2=Leggett|first2=Anne M.|author2-link=Anne M. Leggett|title=Complexities: Women in mathematics|title-link= Complexities: Women in Mathematics |date=31 May 2016|publisher=Princeton University Press|isbn=978-1400880164}}</ref>

She participated in civil rights demonstrations, and her friends and colleagues [[Etta Falconer]] and [[Lee Lorch]] wrote on her death that "With skill, integrity, steadfastness and love she fought [[racism]] and [[sexism]] her entire life, never yielding to the pressures or problems which beset her path".<ref name="Etta Falconer">{{cite news|last1=Falconer|first1=Etta|last2=Lorch|first2=Lee|title=Vivienne Malone-Mayes: In Memoriam|volume=25|url=https://www.agnesscott.edu/lriddle/women/mayes2.htm|access-date=11 March 2017|work=AWM Newsletter|issue=6|publisher=AWM|date=Nov–Dec 1995}}</ref>

As an educator, Malone-Mayes's developed novel methods of teaching mathematics including a program using self-paced audio-tutorials.  Her mathematical research was in the field of [[functional analysis]], particularly characterizing the [[asymptotic analysis|growth properties]] of [[range of a function|ranges]] of [[nonlinear operator]]s. Malone-Mayes graduated in 1966, with a dissertation entitled "A structure problem in asymptotic analysis".<ref name="Warren 1999" />

Following graduation, Malone-Mayes was hired as a full-time professor in the mathematics department at Baylor University. Her research there continued to focus on functional analysis; of her two papers, one studies [[summability methods]] for the [[moment problem]] as operators on [[sequence spaces]]<ref>{{cite journal|title=Some properties of the Leininger generalized Hausdorff matrix|journal=Houston Journal of Mathematics|last1=Mayes|first1=Vivienne|last2=Rhoades|first2=B.&nbsp;E.|volume=6|issue=2|year=1980|citeseerx=10.1.1.589.1897}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|url=https://projecteuclid.org/download/pdf_1/euclid.ijm/1258138149|title=Hausdorff matrices and composition operators|last1=Galanopoulos|first1=Petros|last2=Siskaki|first2=Aristomenos&nbsp;G.|journal=Illinois Journal of Mathematics|volume=45|issue=3|date=Fall 2001|pages=757–773|via=Project Euclid|format=pdf|doi=10.1215/ijm/1258138149|doi-access=free}}</ref> and the other studies the long-term behavior of a certain [[linear ordinary differential equation]].<ref name="Mayes PAMS 1969" />

Nonetheless, her research was sufficiently innovative for her to qualify for federal grants to support her work,<ref name="Warren 1999" /> and the latter paper was published in the prestigious [[Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society]].<ref name="Mayes PAMS 1969">{{cite journal|last1=Mayes|first1=Vivienne|title=Some Steady State Properties of equation 1|journal=Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society|date=September 1969|volume=22|issue=3|pages=672–677|url=https://www.agnesscott.edu/lriddle/women/abstracts/mayes_abstract.htm|access-date=11 March 2017|doi=10.2307/2037456|jstor=2037456|url-access=subscription}}</ref> She was soon a full professor.<ref name="Warren 1999" />

Malone-Mayes had a successful, lengthy career and served on several boards and committees of note, retiring in 1994 due to ill health. She was the fifth African-American woman to be allowed in the White House.<ref name="Vivienne" />

==Memberships==
 
She was a member of the board of directors of the [[National Association of Mathematicians]];<ref name=WH>[https://wacohistory.org/items/show/51  Waco History website, ''Vivienne Lucille Malone-Mayes'', article by Amanda Mylin and Prisca Bird]</ref> she was also elected Director-at-large for the Texas section of [[Mathematical Association of America]] and served as director of the High School Lecture Program for the Texas section.

She was also active in her local community as a lifetime member and musician of New Hope Baptist Church.<ref>[https://www.mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Malone-Mayes/     University of St Andrews website, ''Vivienne Malone-Mayes'']</ref>  She served on boards of directors for [[Cerebral Palsy]], [[Goodwill Industries]], and Family Counseling and Children and was on the Texas State Advisory Council for Construction of Community Mental Health Centers.<ref name=BU /> She also  served on the board of the Heart of Texas Region Mental Health and Mental Retardation Center.<ref name=Vivienne/>

Vivienne Malone-Mayes was a member of [[Delta Sigma Theta]] sorority and served as President of Waco Alumnae Chapter.<ref name=TSHA>[https://www.tshaonline.org/handbook/entries/malone-mayes-vivienne-lucille  Texas State Historical Association Online website, ''Malone-Mayes, Vivienne Lucille'']</ref>

==Legacy and awards==
 
After [[Lillian K. Bradley]] in 1960, Malone-Mayes became one of the first African-American women to receive a PhD in mathematics from [[University of Texas]] (and fifth African-American woman in the United States). She was the first African-American member of the faculty at [[Baylor University]],<ref name=TSHA /> and was also the first African-American person elected to Executive Committee of the [[Association of Women in Mathematics]].

The student congress of Baylor voted her the "Outstanding Faculty Member of the Year" in 1971.<ref name=WH />

==Personal==
Malone married James Mayes in 1952,<ref name="Vivienne" /> and had a daughter, Patsyanne Mayes Wheeler.<ref name="Etta Falconer" />

Malone-Mayes died of a heart attack, in Waco, on June 9, 1995, at the age of 63.<ref name="Etta Falconer" /> She is buried in [[Greenwood Cemetery (Waco)|Greenwood Cemetery]].<ref name="Minutaglio">{{cite book |last=Minutaglio |first=Bill |date=2021 |title=A Single Star and Bloody Knuckles: A History of Politics and Race in Texas |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=lYcHEAAAQBAJ&pg=PA57 |location= |publisher=University of Texas Press |pages=57–62 |isbn=9781477310366}}</ref>
